# redeliver.mdx

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/api-reference/webhooks/redeliver.mdx

title: 'Redeliver'
api: 'POST /api/webhooks/{id}/deliveries/{deliveryId}/redeliver'

Re-send a message to the endpoint. The redelivery carries the **same** `svix-id`, so a receiver that dedupes treats it as the same message. Use it when the original never landed. See [Webhooks](/sandboxes/webhooks#deliveries).

<ParamField path="id" type="string" required>
  Destination ID (`whk_…`).
</ParamField>

<ParamField path="deliveryId" type="string" required>
  Message id (`msg_…`, from [list deliveries](/api-reference/webhooks/deliveries-list)).
</ParamField>

<ResponseExample>
```json 200
{
  "ok": true
}
```
</ResponseExample>

The new attempt appears under [deliveries](/api-reference/webhooks/deliveries-list).

---

# test.mdx

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/api-reference/webhooks/test.mdx

title: 'Test Webhook'
api: 'POST /api/webhooks/{id}/test'

Enqueue a sample event to exercise your endpoint. It sends a real, signed message of a concrete type
the destination is subscribed to (the first of its `eventTypes`, defaulting to `sandbox.created`),
carrying the **normal delivery envelope** with `event.data.test = true` — so you exercise your real
verifier and parser. Delivery is **asynchronous** — this returns once the message is accepted; check
[deliveries](/api-reference/webhooks/deliveries-list) for the outcome.

<Note>
The sample is published through your org's webhook app, so it is **not** isolated to this one
destination: any other destination subscribed to the same event type (and matching scope) also
receives it (likewise marked `event.data.test = true`).
</Note>

See [Webhooks](/sandboxes/webhooks).

<ParamField path="id" type="string" required>
  Destination ID (`whk_…`).
</ParamField>

<ResponseExample>
```json 200
{
  "ok": true,
  "eventType": "sandbox.created",
  "messageId": "msg_2aB…"
}
```
</ResponseExample>

`messageId` is the delivery's message id — find its attempt under [deliveries](/api-reference/webhooks/deliveries-list).

---

# update.mdx

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/api-reference/webhooks/update.mdx

title: 'Update Webhook'
api: 'PATCH /api/webhooks/{id}'

Update a destination — pause/resume, retune filters, change the URL, or rotate the secret. See [Webhooks](/sandboxes/webhooks).

<ParamField path="id" type="string" required>
  Destination ID (`whk_…`).
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="url" type="string">
  New HTTPS endpoint.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="eventTypes" type="string[]">
  Replace the event-type allow-list (unknown types are rejected with `400`). Pass `null` to clear it (deliver all types).
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="enabled" type="boolean">
  Pause (`false`) or resume (`true`) delivery. Pausing does **not** drop events — events that occur while paused are queued and delivered when you re-enable.
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="rotateSecret" type="boolean">
  Rotate to a **new** generated signing secret, returned as `secret` in the response. The previous secret stays valid for a short rollover window so in-flight deliveries still verify. (To set a specific secret, create a new destination.)
</ParamField>

<ParamField body="name" type="string">
  Rename the destination.
</ParamField>

`sandboxId` (scope) is **immutable** — set it at create; it can't be changed here. The current signing secret is re-fetchable any time via [`GET /api/webhooks/{id}/secret`](/api-reference/webhooks/get).

<ResponseExample>
```json 200
{
  "id": "whk_3f9a2c",
  "name": "prod",
  "url": "https://app.example.com/oc-webhook",
  "eventTypes": ["sandbox.stopped", "sandbox.ready"],
  "sandboxId": null,
  "enabled": true,
  "hasSecret": true,
  "createdAt": "2026-06-24T12:00:00Z",
  "updatedAt": "2026-06-24T12:05:00Z"
}
```
</ResponseExample>

---

# opencomputer.toml

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/agents.mdx

title: "Agents"
description: "From a single prompt to a versioned agent defined as code"

<Note>**Preview** — see the [overview](/background-agents/overview); some
capabilities below are still rolling out.</Note>

An agent is configuration, not compute: what it knows (prompt, skills), what
drives it (runtime, model), what wakes it (triggers), what it may do
(policies), and a connection scoping which repos it acts on. Sessions
reference an agent; the agent itself never runs.

An agent is **not bound to a repo or a workspace**. Its connection defines the
*candidate set* of repos it may act on; each session
[resolves](/background-agents/workspaces#resolution-and-sharing) which one(s) to
work in at runtime — from the trigger, the conversation, an optional `repo`
default on the agent, or by asking. This is why one agent can serve issues in
several repos, or hold a chat where it picks the repo from what you ask.

## Start as a prompt

```bash
oc agent create fixer \
  --model anthropic/claude-opus-4-8 \
  --prompt "You fix bugs labeled 'agent' in acme/web." \
  --trigger github:issue.labeled:agent
```

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.opencomputer.dev/v2/agents \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OC_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "fixer",
    "runtime": { "image": "claude", "model": "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8" },
    "prompt": "You fix bugs labeled agent in acme/web.",
    "triggers": [{ "type": "github", "on": "issue.labeled:agent" }]
  }'
```

## Grow into a repo

When one prompt isn't enough, the agent becomes a directory:

```
my-agent/
  opencomputer.toml # name, runtime, model, triggers, policies, connection
  prompt.md
  skills/
    testing.md      # conventions the agent loads when relevant
    deploys.md
  mcp.json          # MCP servers the agent may use
```

```bash
oc agent deploy
```

Keep it in git, review changes as PRs, deploy from CI. The directory and the
API are two views of the same object; GitHub is not required.

```toml
# opencomputer.toml
name = "fixer"

[runtime]
image = "claude"
model = "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8"

[[triggers]]
type = "github"
on = "issue.labeled:agent"

[policies]
budget.per_session_usd = 5
```

## Versions

Every change — config update, deploy, model switch — is a new immutable
version:

```bash
oc agent versions fixer
oc agent diff fixer v3 v4
oc agent rollback fixer v3
```

Sessions pin the version they started with; updates apply to new sessions
only.

## Policies

- **Deliveries** — draft PRs only by default; protected branches are never
  pushed; target repos can be restricted.
- **Actors** — who can trigger work and wake sessions; your organization's
  members by default.
- **Budget** — per-session and per-month caps.
- **Models** — restrict allowed providers.
- **Network** — sandbox egress is allowlist-based.

Organization policies are ceilings: an agent can be stricter, not looser.
Policies live in the versioned config, so every change is a visible diff.

---

# api.mdx

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/api.mdx

title: "API Reference"
description: "The Background Agents REST surface"

<Note>**Preview** — see the [overview](/background-agents/overview); some
endpoints below are still rolling out.</Note>

Base URL `https://api.opencomputer.dev`; authenticate with
`Authorization: Bearer $OC_API_KEY`. The CLI is a wrapper over these calls.

## Agents

```http
POST   /v2/agents                    # create — can be as little as {name, connection, runtime, prompt}
GET    /v2/agents                    # list
GET    /v2/agents/:id
PATCH  /v2/agents/:id                # any config change creates a new version
GET    /v2/agents/:id/versions
POST   /v2/agents/:id/versions      # deploy a bundle (what `oc agent deploy` calls)
```

```json
{
  "name": "fixer",
  "connection": "github:acme",
  "runtime": { "image": "claude", "model": "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8" },
  "prompt": "You fix bugs labeled 'agent' in acme/web.",
  "triggers": [
    { "type": "github", "on": "issue.labeled:agent",
      "route": { "key": "issue.{number}", "mode": "reuse" } }
  ],
  "policies": { "budget": { "per_session_usd": 5 } }
}
```

## Workspaces

Keyed by the repo(s) they prepare, not by agent — a session
[resolves](/background-agents/workspaces#resolution-and-sharing) which repo(s)
to work in (from the trigger, the conversation, a default, or by asking) and
matches a workspace covering that repo and ref.

```http
POST   /v2/workspaces                # { name, recipe: {repos: [{repo, ref?}], setup[], warm[]}, refresh, pool }
GET    /v2/workspaces?repo=&ref=     # list / resolve by repo and ref
GET    /v2/workspaces/:id            # recipe, pool status, latest build
GET    /v2/workspaces/:id/builds     # immutable lineage
POST   /v2/workspaces/:id/builds     # build now
```

## Sessions

```http
POST   /v2/sessions                  # { agent, input?, key? } — start explicitly
GET    /v2/sessions?agent=&status=   # list / filter
GET    /v2/sessions/:id              # status, pins, sandbox info, usage
PATCH  /v2/sessions/:id              # { model_override } — this session only, audited
GET    /v2/sessions/:id/events       # ?after=<cursor>&stream=sse&level=user
POST   /v2/sessions/:id/events      # raw append (low-level): [{ kind: "message", body: "..." }]
POST   /v2/sessions/:id/archive
```

`status` is `active | dormant | awaiting_input | archived` (`awaiting_input` =
the agent emitted an `ask` and yielded).

Session object (abridged):

```json
{
  "id": "s_8f2…",
  "status": "dormant",
  "pins": {
    "agent_version": 4,
    "workspace_build": 14,
    "runtime": "claude@sha256:…",
    "model": { "requested": "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8", "served": "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8" }
  },
  "sandbox": { "state": "hibernated", "preview_urls": [] },
  "usage": { "active_seconds": 672, "tokens": { "in": 184211, "out": 9302 }, "usd": 0.47 }
}
```

Event envelope — every event carries a `level`
([visibility class](/background-agents/observability#levels)):

```json
{
  "id": "evt_01…",
  "ts": "2026-06-12T09:31:04Z",
  "actor": "platform",
  "kind": "delivery",
  "level": "user",
  "target": "chan_…",
  "body": { "type": "pr.open", "repo": "acme/web", "number": 413, "as": "maria" },
  "refs": [{ "type": "github_pr", "number": 413 }]
}
```

Kinds: `message`, `say`, `action`, `ask`, `delivery`, `status`, `timer`,
`exec.completed`, `error`. Levels: `internal | progress | user`, derived at
append from `(actor, kind)` with an optional override. `target` (optional) names
a [channel binding](#messaging) to deliver an event to a specific thread.

## Messaging

The two-way surface a chat UI is built on — send messages in, render the stream
out, bind external threads (see [Channels](/background-agents/channels)):

```http
POST   /v2/sessions/:id/messages     # a steer (in): { text, actor?, idem_key? }
GET    /v2/sessions/:id/messages?after=…    # conversation history (replay a UI)
POST   /v2/sessions/:id/channels     # bind a thread: { provider, thread_ref, role[] }
GET    /v2/sessions/:id/channels     # list bindings
```

`POST /messages` is the ergonomic steer (one inbound message); `POST /events`
is the low-level raw append underneath it. Channel `role[]` is
`conversation | delivery`.

<Note>**Preview** — `POST /v2/sessions/:id/interrupt` (mid-turn interrupt
steering) is designed but not built in v0. Steers are consumed at the next turn
boundary; see [Sessions](/background-agents/sessions#preview-mid-turn-interrupt).</Note>

## Connections & models

```http
POST   /v2/connections               # { type: "github" | "github_user" | "slack" | "anthropic" | "openai", ... }
GET    /v2/connections
GET    /v2/models                    # aggregated catalog from connected providers
```

The `slack` connection (per-workspace OAuth, token held platform-side) powers
the [Slack channel](/background-agents/channels). In v0 it is
platform-configured for a single workspace; self-serve `oc connect slack` is
Preview.

## Observability

```http
GET    /v2/sessions/:id/turns
GET    /v2/sessions/:id/turns/:tid/trace
GET    /v2/sessions/:id/logs?turn=
GET    /v2/sessions/:id/model-calls?turn=
```

---

# opencomputer.toml

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/channels.mdx

title: "Channels"
description: "Two-way conversation — talk to an agent in Slack, watch it work, steer it"

<Note>**Preview** — see the [overview](/background-agents/overview); some
capabilities below are still rolling out. Slack is the first channel and is
live in v0 (single, platform-configured workspace — see [State](#state)).</Note>

A session is not just a record you read after the fact — it is a two-way
thread you can talk to. A **channel** connects that thread to a place people
already work: a Slack thread, a GitHub PR. The same session can be reached
from several places at once; you never have to declare it "a Slack agent" or
"a GitHub agent."

Target experience: *"@agent the build's failing — take a look"* in a Slack
thread. The agent replies in-thread, narrates what it's doing, asks when it
needs a decision, opens a draft PR — and a comment on that PR is just another
message into the **same** session.

## Slack as a channel

A Slack-triggered agent declares one trigger — that is the whole thing. The
agent that declares the Slack trigger *is* the Slack agent:

```toml
# opencomputer.toml
name = "slack-helper"

[runtime]
image = "claude"
model = "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8"

[[triggers]]
type = "slack"          # an @mention starts or continues a thread-session
on   = "mention"

[connection]
github = "diggerhq"     # the repos it may act on (it resolves which from the chat)
```

`@mention` it in a channel and it starts a session bound to that Slack thread;
replies in the thread continue the same session. The agent resolves which repo
to work in from the conversation (see [Workspaces](/background-agents/workspaces#resolution-and-sharing)),
investigates in a sandbox, and opens a draft PR — reporting back in the thread
throughout. The full example is [`slack-helper`](/background-agents/quickstart).

## How it flows

- **Ingress.** Slack delivers the mention/reply to the platform's `/gw/slack`
  endpoint; it is verified, de-duplicated by Slack's event id, and appended to
  the session's timeline as a **steer** (an inbound message — see
  [Conversation](/background-agents/sessions#conversation)).
- **Routing.** A **channel binding** ties the session to the Slack
  `channel + thread_ts`. The platform finds the session by that binding (or
  creates one), so every later reply lands on the same thread.
- **Projection.** The platform's **outbox** posts the agent's outbound events
  back to the thread — durably and idempotently, retrying through any provider
  blip. What gets shown is controlled by event
  [level](/background-agents/observability#levels): `user` messages and `ask`
  questions post as replies; `progress` narration can be coalesced into a
  single live "working…" message.

The agent never calls Slack itself. It only appends events; the platform
projects them. The same machinery serves any provider — GitHub is the other
instance of this contract today.

## Bindings are additive — no forced surface

A session has a *set* of bindings, added over its life — never a fixed type:

- A Slack-born session that opens a PR gains a **delivery** binding to that PR;
  the PR links back to the same session.
- A session can be surfaced in more than one place — the model does not force a
  choice between "Slack" and "GitHub."

Routing follows event level: conversation (`user`/`progress`) goes to
conversation bindings, work product (`delivery`) goes to delivery targets. An
event may name a specific binding to override (e.g. answer on the PR rather
than in Slack).

<Note>**Preview** — a GitHub PR comment flowing back into a chat-born session
as *conversation* is designed but not built in v0: today PR comments wake the
session that opened the PR (delivery), and Slack is the conversation channel.
The binding model above is built so this is a later addition, not a redesign.</Note>

## Build your own surface

Slack is one consumer of a small public API — the same surface a custom UI is
built on (see the [API](/background-agents/api#messaging)):

```http
POST /v2/sessions/:id/messages   # send a message in (a steer)
GET  /v2/sessions/:id/events?stream=sse&level=user   # render the thread out
POST /v2/sessions/:id/channels   # bind a thread { provider, thread_ref, role[] }
```

Post messages in, render the event stream at the level you want, optionally
bind a thread so the platform projects for you. Building a chat UI on a session
is an afternoon.

## State

- **v0 (live):** Slack ingress + projection, additive bindings, the outbox,
  `ask`/answer, and cheap-visible resilience (kill the sandbox mid-thread and
  the conversation resumes, nothing dropped). Single workspace,
  **platform-configured** for the demo.
- **Preview / planned:** `oc connect slack` self-serve OAuth and multiple Slack
  workspaces; PR-comment-as-conversation into a chat-born session; channels
  beyond Slack (Discord, email, web); recovering messages sent while the
  platform was down by reconciling against channel history.

---

# how-it-works.mdx

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/how-it-works.mdx

title: "How it works"
description: "The moving parts, how they interact, and why they're split this way"

<Note>**Preview** — see the [overview](/background-agents/overview); some
capabilities below are still rolling out.</Note>

<Frame>
  <img src="/images/background-agents-architecture.svg" alt="Background Agents architecture: triggers feed a durable session timeline; a disposable runtime reads and appends to it, calls models through the gateway, and acts in a disposable sandbox; deliveries carry results back to GitHub" />
</Frame>

## The moving parts

| Part | What it is | Durability | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| Session timeline | Append-only event record in the platform | **Durable** — it *is* the session | Holds everything that happened; wakes the runtime when new events arrive |
| Runtime | A VM running the agent loop | Disposable | Read timeline → call model → decide → act. Holds no state, no credentials |
| Model gateway *(Preview)* | Proxy between runtimes and providers | **Durable** (its records) | As designed: applies the configured model per call, holds provider keys, meters tokens, records every request and response as they stream — encrypted, used only to resume the session, never exposed unless capture is opted in. Not built in v0 |
| Sandbox | A VM booted from the workspace's latest build | Disposable (snapshotted periodically) | Where the agent acts: commands, edits, tests. One per session, never shared |
| Connectors & outbox | Platform-side GitHub/Slack integration | **Durable** (delivery state) | Carry events out — open PRs and post comments, project the agent's messages into Slack/PR threads — at-least-once and idempotent, attributed to the requesting user. Also bring inbound messages in as steers |

## How a task flows

1. Someone labels an issue. The trigger event is stored on a session's
   timeline (new session, or the existing one for that issue).
2. The platform starts a runtime and attaches the session's sandbox.
3. The runtime reads the timeline from where it left off and calls the
   model — through the gateway, which substitutes the configured model and
   records the exchange.
4. The agent acts in the sandbox; each action is appended to the timeline
   as it happens.
5. To open a PR, the runtime appends a delivery request; a connector
   performs it and records the PR number.
6. Nothing left to do: the runtime exits, the sandbox sleeps. The session is
   dormant — just the record, no machines; storage only.
7. A comment on the PR routes back to this session (step 5 recorded the PR),
   and the cycle repeats with full context.

## Two-way flow

The timeline is a bus in both directions, not just an output log:

- **In.** Any inbound message — a Slack reply, a PR comment, an API call — is a
  **steer**: appended to the timeline (de-duplicated by the provider's event id)
  and consumed at the next turn. A **channel binding** ties the session to an
  external thread (a Slack `thread_ts`, a PR number) so follow-ups land on the
  same session. Bindings are additive — a session is never typed by surface.
- **Out.** The agent speaks with `say` (a message) and `ask` (a question that
  pauses the turn until answered). The **outbox** projects these — and
  deliveries — to the bound channels, at-least-once and idempotent, so a
  replayed turn after a crash never double-posts and a provider blip never drops
  a message. The agent only appends events; it never calls Slack or GitHub
  itself.

See [Channels](/background-agents/channels) and the
[conversation model](/background-agents/sessions#conversation).

## Why it's split this way

Both machines are disposable because no state lives in them — it has already
left by the time it could be lost:

- events are stored as they are produced (step 4);
- the conversation is recorded at the gateway (step 3) — provider APIs carry
  the full context on every call, so the latest recorded exchange is the
  agent's complete working memory *(gateway recording is Preview; see the
  note above)*;
- sandbox files are snapshotted periodically while work is in progress.

What this buys (gateway-dependent points are Preview, not built in v0):

- **Crash-proof.** Kill either machine mid-task and the session resumes where
  it was on fresh machines. As designed, even a kill mid-model-call recovers:
  the in-flight response is still recorded at the gateway, and not re-billed.
- **Free dormancy.** Waiting detaches both machines; a session can sleep for
  months for ~storage cost and wake in seconds.
- **Model switching as configuration.** As designed, the gateway applies
  model config on each request — no restart. Within a provider, a change is
  effective on the next call; switching providers is effective on the next
  turn, when the runtime reconnects. Keys never enter the machines.
- **Risk isolation.** The sandbox runs arbitrary code, so it's per-session
  and replaceable; the loop carries neither that risk nor that lifecycle. A
  one-hour build in the sandbox doesn't keep a loop machine running.
- **Safe upgrades.** Sessions pin their agent version, workspace build, and
  runtime at start; changes apply to new sessions.

---

# models.mdx

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/models.mdx

title: "Models"
description: "Provider-prefixed IDs, switched as configuration"

<Note>**Preview** — see the [overview](/background-agents/overview); some
capabilities below are still rolling out.</Note>

The model is configuration on the agent — not part of code or a runtime
image. A change takes effect on the next model call — the next turn, when
switching providers; nothing restarts.

<Note>**Preview** — the hot-swap and metering behavior on this page runs through
the model gateway, which is **not enabled in v0** (see the
[overview](/background-agents/overview)). Today the `claude` runtime calls the
provider directly with a configured key; model addressing and per-agent
configuration are real, but live rewrite, cross-provider flips, and gateway
metering are the designed behavior.</Note>

## Addressing

Provider-prefixed, provider-native IDs:

```
anthropic/claude-opus-4-8
openai/gpt-5.x
```

OpenComputer adds no model names of its own. Bare IDs are accepted when
unambiguous.

```bash
oc model list     # every model available through your connected providers
```

## Switching

```bash
oc agent update fixer --model openai/gpt-5.x    # new agent version
oc session set <id> --model openai/gpt-5.x      # one session, in flight
```

Agent-level changes are versions; session-level overrides appear as `status`
events on the timeline; usage records the model that served each call.
Switching to a different provider requires a [runtime](/background-agents/runtimes)
that drives it (the planned `opencode` drives all — Preview).

## Provider keys

```bash
oc connect anthropic --api-key sk-ant-...
oc connect openai --api-key sk-...
```

Bring your own keys per provider, or run **Managed** (billed to your OpenComputer credits) where available.

As designed, keys never enter agent machines: model traffic flows through
OpenComputer's model gateway, which holds the keys, enforces the configured
model, and meters tokens per session. The gateway is a Preview capability —
see the [overview](/background-agents/overview).

## Restricting

Organizations can restrict allowed providers
([policies](/background-agents/agents#policies)); agent data goes only to
providers you allow.

---

# t_7   2m41s   anthropic/claude-opus-4-8   31.2k tok   $0.41   yielded: delivered PR #413

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/observability.mdx

title: "Observability"
description: "Timeline, turns, model calls, machine output — all correlated"

<Note>**Preview** — see the [overview](/background-agents/overview); some
capabilities below are still rolling out.</Note>

Background agents work unattended; everything they do is recorded and
correlated. From any point on a session's timeline you can drill down to the
model calls and commands behind it.

## Timeline

The durable record: [events](/background-agents/sessions#events) for every
message, action, question, delivery, and error.

```bash
oc session attach <id>                    # live
oc session events <id> --after <cursor>   # history, paginated
```

```bash
curl "https://api.opencomputer.dev/v2/sessions/$ID/events?stream=sse" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OC_API_KEY"
```

## Levels

Every event carries a **level** — a visibility class — and the stream carries
**everything**, full fidelity. You filter; the platform never decides for you
what to show your users.

| Level | What | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `internal` | Platform/runtime mechanics, raw tool I/O | `action` (a tool call), model-call marks |
| `progress` | The play-by-play — "watch it work" | agent narration, `status` ("cloned repo", "running tests") |
| `user` | What an end-user sees by default | the agent's `say`, `ask`, and `delivery` ("opened PR #42") |

The stream filters by a **minimum** level — `?level=user` is just the
conversation; `?level=progress` adds narration; `?level=internal` is everything
(the debug view). Default is full fidelity.

```bash
oc session attach <id> --level user
```

```bash
curl "https://api.opencomputer.dev/v2/sessions/$ID/events?stream=sse&level=progress" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OC_API_KEY"
```

This is how a [channel](/background-agents/channels) decides what to surface: a
Slack thread renders `user`/`progress`, a debugging view renders `internal`
too — from the one stream.

## Turns

A turn is one stretch of activity (wake → work → sleep):

```bash
oc session turns <id>
# t_7   2m41s   anthropic/claude-opus-4-8   31.2k tok   $0.41   yielded: delivered PR #413
oc session trace <id> t_7        # spans: model calls, commands, deliveries, timings
oc session logs <id> --turn t_7  # raw runtime output
oc session model-calls <id>      # per call: provider, model served, tokens, latency
```

Command output appears on the timeline as `action` events, truncated inline
with full output downloadable.

## Cost

```bash
oc session get <id>    # usage: active_seconds, tokens, usd
```

Metered per session and per turn. Dormant time is absent because it isn't
billed.

## Model traffic privacy

By default, model-call metadata (model, tokens, latency, cost) is recorded;
prompt and response contents are not exposed. Payload capture is opt-in per
agent (`capture_model_io`) and surfaces in `oc session model-calls --full`.

<Note>**Preview** — payload capture runs through the model gateway, which is not
enabled in v0 (see the [overview](/background-agents/overview)). Until then,
only metadata is available; the `capture_model_io` opt-in and `--full` payloads
are the designed behavior.</Note>

## Debugging

1. `oc session attach` — what did it do and say?
2. `oc session trace` — where did time and tokens go?
3. `oc session shell` — open the machine.
4. `oc session state download` — export the working context to reproduce
   the run locally in the same harness.

---

# overview.mdx

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/overview.mdx

title: "Background Agents"
description: "Event-triggered agents with durable sessions, on managed compute"

<Note>
**Preview.** Background Agents is in active development. This section
describes the product as designed; capabilities are rolling out in stages and
not all are generally available yet. Commands are shown in the target grammar
`oc agent …`; today they ship under the `oc-agents` CLI (e.g. `oc-agents agent
deploy`), because the `oc agent …` namespace currently belongs to
[Hosted Agents](/agent-sessions/overview). The runtime that ships today is
`claude`; the gateway-dependent capabilities (model hot-swap, payload capture)
and prepared workspaces are flagged Preview where they appear.
</Note>

A background agent works unattended: an issue gets labeled, the agent fixes
it in a fresh machine and opens a draft PR. A comment on that PR a day later
wakes the same agent with full context. You pay for the minutes it worked.

Background Agents runs everything around the agent loop: event ingestion,
session state, machine preparation, delivery back to GitHub, metering. The
model — or the entire harness — is a configuration change.

## Concepts

| Concept | What it is |
|---|---|
| [Agent](/background-agents/agents) | Definition: prompt, skills, model, triggers, policies, and a connection. Versioned. Not bound to a repo or workspace; via its connection it acts across many repos. |
| [Session](/background-agents/sessions) | One thread of work: a durable event timeline. Active while working, dormant otherwise; dormant holds no compute. |
| [Workspace](/background-agents/workspaces) | A prepared environment for one or more repos, rebuilt on every push — dependencies installed, build warm. Not tied to an agent. |
| [Trigger](/background-agents/triggers) | GitHub events or a Slack @mention, routed to the right session. |
| [Channel](/background-agents/channels) | A two-way thread the session talks in — Slack today, a GitHub PR. Bindings are additive; a session is never typed by surface. |
| [Connection](/background-agents/triggers#connections) | The GitHub App install, Slack workspace, and model provider keys. |
| [Runtime](/background-agents/runtimes) | The loop that drives a session. Its model is separate configuration. |

## How it works

A session is a durable timeline of events. While there is work, two machines
attach: a **runtime** (the loop) and a **sandbox** (the machine it acts in);
they detach when the work pauses. All state — events, the model
conversation, files — leaves the machines as it is produced, so either can
die at any point and the session resumes where it was. Details:
[How it works](/background-agents/how-it-works).

## Relation to sandboxes

Sessions work inside ordinary [sandboxes](/sandboxes/overview), booted from
the workspace's latest build and managed for you. `oc session shell <id>`
opens the actual machine. For full control of the loop and the machine, use
the [Agent SDK](/agent-sessions/overview) instead. [Hosted
Agents](/agent-sessions/overview) remains the surface for chat-style agents on
managed cores and channels; Background Agents is for event-triggered,
unattended work.

## Properties

- Sessions start in seconds, because the workspace rebuilt itself on the
  last push.
- Models are addressed `provider/model` and switched with one command —
  effective on the next call within a provider, on the next turn across
  providers. Bring your own keys, or run Managed (billed to your credits).
- Agents hold no tokens. The platform opens PRs and posts comments on their
  behalf, attributed to the requesting user.
- Sessions are two-way. Talk to an agent in a Slack thread, watch it work, and
  steer it; it asks when it needs a decision. See
  [Channels](/background-agents/channels).

[Quickstart →](/background-agents/quickstart)

---

# opencomputer.toml

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/quickstart.mdx

title: "Quickstart"
description: "A working background agent in three commands"

After this page, labeling a GitHub issue `agent` produces a draft PR, and
commenting on that PR wakes the same agent to follow up.

<Note>**Preview** — see the [overview](/background-agents/overview); some steps
below are still rolling out.</Note>

## 1. Connect GitHub

```bash
oc connect github
```

Installs the OpenComputer GitHub App on your org. No app registration,
webhook setup, or secrets. To have PRs open **as you** rather than as the App
on your behalf, also run `oc connect github --as-user`.

## 2. Create a workspace (optional, Preview)

```bash
oc workspace create web \
  --repo github.com/acme/web \
  --setup "pnpm i && pnpm build"
```

A workspace prepares a repo ahead of time: the first build clones it, runs
setup, and snapshots the result, then rebuilds on every push so sessions
start from a ready machine matching the latest code. `oc workspace builds
web` lists the builds. **In v0 this step is not built yet** — skip it and the
session clones the repo on demand.

## 3. Create the agent

```bash
oc agent create fixer \
  --model anthropic/claude-opus-4-8 \
  --prompt "You fix bugs labeled 'agent' in acme/web. Keep diffs minimal. Run the affected tests before pushing." \
  --trigger github:issue.labeled:agent
```

## Use it

Label an issue `agent`. A session starts within seconds:

```bash
oc session list --agent fixer
oc session attach <session-id>   # live events; Ctrl-C detaches, the agent keeps working
```

A draft PR opens, attributed to the person who labeled the issue — as them if
they ran `oc connect github --as-user`, otherwise opened by the App on their
behalf. The session goes dormant; `oc session get <id>` shows `usage.active_seconds` — dormant time
uses no compute.

Comment on the PR: *"also update the changelog."* The session wakes with its
full context, pushes a commit, and sleeps again. The thread persists; a
comment weeks later wakes the same context.

## Change the model

```bash
oc agent update fixer --model openai/gpt-5.x
```

Effective when the agent next wakes — switching providers means the runtime
reconnects; a change within the same provider applies on the very next model
call. Same prompt and triggers. Each change is a new agent
version — `oc agent rollback fixer v1` reverts.

## Or: talk to it in Slack

An agent can be conversational instead of (or as well as) issue-triggered.
Declare a Slack trigger and it becomes a teammate you @mention in a thread:

```toml
# opencomputer.toml
name = "slack-helper"

[runtime]
image = "claude"
model = "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8"

[[triggers]]
type = "slack"
on   = "mention"

[connection]
github = "diggerhq"   # the repos it may act on; it resolves which from the chat
```

```bash
oc connect slack          # install the OpenComputer Slack app (Preview — see below)
oc agent deploy ./slack-helper
```

`/invite` it to a channel and @mention it:

```
you   @slack-helper parseDuration in oc-agent-demo-target mis-parses "1.5h" — fix it?
bot   On it — pulling oc-agent-demo-target…
bot   Found it: the regex silently drops "1.". Throw on bad input, or support fractions?
you   throw
bot   Done — tests pass. 📦 Opened PR #42
```

It works out *which* repo from the conversation, investigates in a sandbox,
**asks** when it needs a decision (and pauses, free, until you reply), and opens
a draft PR — narrating in-thread the whole time. Full walkthrough:
[Channels](/background-agents/channels).

<Note>**Preview** — in v0 the Slack app is platform-configured for a single demo
workspace; self-serve `oc connect slack` is planned.</Note>

## Next

- [Agents as code](/background-agents/agents)
- [Sessions and dormancy](/background-agents/sessions)
- [Workspace freshness and warm pools](/background-agents/workspaces)

---

# claude      Claude Code / Agent SDK harness (default)

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/runtimes.mdx

title: "Runtimes"
description: "The loop that drives a session, selected like a base image"

<Note>**Preview** — see the [overview](/background-agents/overview); some
capabilities below are still rolling out.</Note>

The runtime is the agent loop: it reads the session, calls the model, and
acts in the session's machine. You select it; OpenComputer operates it.

```toml
[runtime]
image = "claude"
model = "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8"
```

```bash
oc runtime list
# claude      Claude Code / Agent SDK harness (default)
# codex       Preview — not built yet
# opencode    Preview — multi-provider harness, not built yet
```

## Semantics

- **Versioned like a deployment.** Tags move, digests pin; each session
  records the digest it runs, so runtime upgrades never affect in-flight
  sessions.
- **The model is not part of the runtime** — it's
  [configuration](/background-agents/models). Runtimes declare which
  providers they can drive; switching *across* providers needs an image that
  drives the target (the planned `opencode` drives all — Preview).
- **Stateless and disposable.** Session state — conversation, timeline,
  sandbox files — lives outside the runtime. If a runtime's machine dies
  mid-task, the session continues on a fresh one; the timeline shows an
  `error` event and a short pause.
- **No credentials.** By design, model keys stay in the gateway (a Preview
  capability) and delivery tokens in the platform.

## Behavior

- **No busy-waiting.** Waiting — on a person, a long build, the clock —
  makes the session dormant instead of burning compute.
- **Asks yield.** When the agent needs a decision it emits an `ask` and the
  turn yields; the session goes `awaiting_input` and holds no compute until a
  reply arrives (`oc session send`).
- **Budget-aware.** Runtimes wind down near the session's budget cap; the
  platform enforces the cap regardless.

## Tools the runtime provides

The agent works through a small set of platform tools — building an agent is
mostly a prompt that uses them well:

- **`say`** / **`ask`** — speak to the human; the agent's raw reasoning is never
  shown, only `say`/`ask`. `ask` pauses the turn until answered (see
  [Conversation](/background-agents/sessions#conversation)).
- **`use_repo`** — pick a repo to work in from the ones the connection covers,
  and switch or open more
  ([resolution](/background-agents/workspaces#resolution-and-sharing)).
- **`deliver`** — open or update a draft PR; the platform pushes it as the
  human, so no git tokens enter the sandbox.
- **`bash` / `read` / `write` / `ls`** — the session's sandbox.

<Note>**Preview** — additional platform images (`codex`, `opencode`) and
publishing your own loop (`oc runtime push`) use the same registry and contract,
but are not built in v0; `claude` is the runtime that ships today.</Note>

---

# sessions.mdx

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/sessions.mdx

title: "Sessions"
description: "Durable threads of work; dormant sessions hold no compute"

<Note>**Preview** — see the [overview](/background-agents/overview); some
capabilities below are still rolling out.</Note>

A session is one thread of an agent's work: one issue, one PR, one ongoing
conversation. It is an append-only **event timeline**, durable independently
of any machine. Compute attaches when there is work and detaches when there
isn't.

## Lifecycle

```
active ◄──► dormant ──► archived (retention policy)
   │
   └──► awaiting_input (waiting on a human answer)
```

- **active** — a runtime is working; billing runs.
- **dormant** — nothing to do. No compute attached; storage only. A
  session can stay dormant for months and wake in seconds.
- **awaiting_input** — the agent asked a question (`ask`) and is waiting. The
  turn has yielded, so no compute is attached; a reply wakes it.
- Sessions are never forcibly ended; archival is a retention policy you set.

Machine failures, deploys, and restarts do not lose session state. Kill the
sandbox mid-thread and the session resumes — a dead-but-connectable machine is
recreated and re-cloned, and the pushed branch plus the event timeline are the
durable copy of the work; nothing in the conversation is dropped. *(As
designed, the conversation also resumes byte-exact from the gateway's recorded
exchange — a [Preview](/background-agents/overview) capability, not built in v0;
the cheap-visible resume above is what ships today.)*

## Starting and routing

Sessions start from triggers, or explicitly:

```bash
oc session start fixer "migrate the date helpers to Temporal"
```

Triggers route by **routing key** — by default one session per GitHub
issue. Follow-ups find their session: a comment on a PR resumes the session
that opened it. One agent runs many concurrent sessions.

## Conversation

A session is two-way. The agent has two ways to reach a human, and only these
two are shown — its raw internal reasoning is never surfaced:

- **`say`** — a deliberate message to the human: progress, a finding, an
  answer. The frontend chooses how much to surface (see
  [levels](/background-agents/observability#levels)).
- **`ask`** — a question that **pauses the turn**. The agent appends the
  question and yields; the session goes **`awaiting_input`** and holds no
  compute while it waits. A reply wakes it with the answer already in context,
  and it continues. This is what makes it a conversation, not a fire-and-forget
  command.

Any inbound message — a Slack reply, a PR comment, a direct API call — is a
**steer**: it is appended to the timeline and picked up at the next turn. (A
steer adjusts the *next* turn; mid-turn interruption is
[Preview](#preview-mid-turn-interrupt).) Channels project `say`/`ask` and
progress out to where people are watching — see
[Channels](/background-agents/channels).

## Events

Every event carries an actor, a `kind`, and a **`level`** —
`internal | progress | user` — a visibility class so a consumer can show as
much or as little as it wants (see
[Observability](/background-agents/observability#levels)).

| Kind | Level | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `message` | progress | A human or trigger said something; or agent narration |
| `say` | user | The agent's deliberate user-facing message |
| `action` | internal | The agent ran a command or edited files in its sandbox |
| `ask` | user | The agent needs a human decision; the session goes `awaiting_input` until answered |
| `delivery` | user | An outward action performed for the agent — PR opened, comment posted |
| `status` | progress | Lifecycle and configuration changes |
| `timer` | — | A scheduled wake fired |
| `exec.completed` | — | A long-running command the agent was waiting on finished |
| `error` | user | A failure, with retry context |

```bash
oc session attach <id>      # live stream; detaching doesn't stop the agent
oc session send <id> "use the staging DB for repro"   # a steer, in
```

```bash
curl "https://api.opencomputer.dev/v2/sessions/$ID/events?stream=sse" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OC_API_KEY"
```

## The sandbox underneath

Each session works in its own [sandbox](/sandboxes/overview), booted from
the workspace's latest build, managed for you:

```bash
oc session get <id>      # status, pins, sandbox state, preview URLs, usage
oc session shell <id>    # open the actual machine
```

`pins` records what the session runs on — agent version, workspace build,
runtime — so in-flight work is unaffected by updates and runs are
reproducible.

## Cost

You pay for attached compute and model tokens while the session is active
(`usage.active_seconds`). A session that worked 11 minutes across two days
bills 11 minutes of compute; dormant time costs only the storage of the
timeline and snapshots.

## Preview: mid-turn interrupt

A steer is consumed at the next turn boundary — it adjusts the *next* turn, not
the one in flight. Interrupting a turn already running (a steer that redirects
work mid-task) is designed but not built in v0. To steer in v0, send the
message; it is applied when the current turn yields.

---

# triggers.mdx

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/triggers.mdx

title: "Triggers & Connections"
description: "Events in, results out"

<Note>**Preview** — see the [overview](/background-agents/overview); some
capabilities below are still rolling out.</Note>

Triggers bring events to your agent; deliveries carry its work back out.
Both run through **connections** — integrations OpenComputer operates.

## Connections

```bash
oc connect github            # install the OpenComputer GitHub App on your org
oc connect github --as-user  # optional personal grant: deliveries act as you
```

Installing the App is the entire GitHub integration — no app registration,
webhook configuration, or secrets. Model provider keys are also connections;
see [Models](/background-agents/models).

A **Slack** connection (per-workspace OAuth, token held platform-side) powers
the Slack conversation [channel](/background-agents/channels).

```bash
oc connect slack             # install the OpenComputer Slack app to your workspace
```

<Note>**Preview** — in v0 the Slack app is **platform-configured** for a single
demo workspace; self-serve `oc connect slack` and multiple workspaces are
planned. See the [overview](/background-agents/overview).</Note>

## Triggers

Declared on the agent:

```toml
[[triggers]]
type = "github"
on = "issue.labeled:agent"
```

Supported GitHub events include issue labels and PR/issue comments. Events are
acknowledged instantly, then routed:

- **Routing keys** group events into sessions — by default one session per
  issue.
- A comment on a PR the agent opened resumes the session that opened it.

Only members of your organization can trigger an agent or wake a session —
labels and comments from anyone else are ignored. Configurable per agent
([policies](/background-agents/agents#policies)).

### Slack

A `slack` trigger makes the agent conversational — an `@mention` starts or
continues a thread-session:

```toml
[[triggers]]
type = "slack"
on   = "mention"
```

The agent that declares this trigger *is* the Slack agent: mentions and thread
replies route to it as steers, and it talks back in the thread. See
[Channels](/background-agents/channels) for the full two-way model and
[`slack-helper`](/background-agents/quickstart) for a complete example.

<Note>**Preview** — `cron` and `http`/email triggers are planned, not built in
v0.</Note>

## Deliveries

Agents hold no GitHub tokens. To open a PR or post a comment, the agent
requests a **delivery** and the platform performs it:

- With a personal grant, the PR is opened **as the person who triggered the
  work** — review attribution and permissions behave as if they pushed it.
- Without a grant, the App opens it with *"on behalf of @user"* attribution.
- Defaults: draft PRs only, never to protected branches
  ([policies](/background-agents/agents#policies)).

Every delivery appears on the session timeline, and the PR links back to its
session.

---

# #14  4 minutes ago   main@9f3c21  ok   6m12s

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/background-agents/workspaces.mdx

title: "Workspaces"
description: "Prepared environments for one or more repos, rebuilt on every push"

<Note>**Preview** — workspaces are not built in v0 yet. Today a session clones
its repo on demand; the prepared-environment model below describes the
designed behavior. See the [overview](/background-agents/overview).</Note>

Cloning, installing, and building take minutes. A workspace does that work
ahead of time — on every push — and snapshots the result, so sessions boot
into a ready machine in seconds.

A workspace is a first-class resource, not an agent attribute: it prepares
**one or more repos** (each at an optional ref or branch) and is shared by
every agent and session that lands on those repos.

```bash
oc workspace create web \
  --repo github.com/acme/web \
  --setup "pnpm i && pnpm build" \
  --warm "pnpm test --filter smoke" \
  --pool 1
```

## Recipe

- **repo** — one or more repos, cloned via your GitHub connection (read
  access). Each may pin an optional ref or branch; pass `--repo` again to
  span several repos in one environment.
- **setup** — install, build, generate.
- **warm** *(optional)* — run once to heat caches, e.g. a smoke test.

## Builds

The workspace rebuilds on every push to the default branch — clone, setup,
warm, snapshot — so the latest build matches the latest code. `--refresh
30m` switches to interval rebuilds instead: useful at commit volumes where
per-push builds would pile up, or to pick up floating dependencies on a
quiet repo. Builds form an immutable lineage:

```bash
oc workspace builds web
# #14  4 minutes ago   main@9f3c21  ok   6m12s
# #13  34 minutes ago  main@8e1d09  ok   6m05s
```

Sessions boot from the latest successful build and pin it. A failed build
never becomes latest.

Builds run on ordinary sandboxes and bill as build minutes. On-push refresh
costs nothing while the repo is quiet; `--refresh 30m` runs ~48 builds a day
whether or not anything changed.

`--pool N` keeps N machines pre-booted from the latest build, removing even
the boot seconds for busy agents.

## Resolution and sharing

A session is **not bound to a repo** — it *resolves* which repo(s) to work in,
from one of several sources:

- the **triggering event** (a labeled issue's repo) — one source, not the only
  one;
- the **conversation** — a chat-born session has no triggering repo, so the
  agent picks one from the repos its connection covers (see below);
- a **configured default** on the agent;
- or it **asks** the human.

Resolution can be **lazy** (deferred until first needed) and **re-resolvable**:
a session can switch repos mid-thread, or open several at once — each is checked
out as its own directory inside the session's single sandbox.

The agent drives this at runtime with a **`use_repo`** tool: it lists the repos
its [connection](/background-agents/triggers#connections) scopes, checks one
out, and calls again to switch or to add a second checkout. Where a prepared
workspace covers the resolved repo/ref, the session boots from its latest build
(fast); otherwise it **clones on demand**.

Workspaces are not 1:1 with a repo: a repo can have more than one (e.g. per
branch), and a single workspace can span multiple repos. Any workspace covering
a session's repo/ref is shared by every agent and session that lands there,
independent of which agent runs.

## During a session

The workspace defines the machine at session start; after that the session's
sandbox evolves freely. Work in progress is protected independently — if a
session's machine is lost, it is restored with its recent state, not rebuilt
from the workspace (see [Sessions](/background-agents/sessions)).

## API

```bash
POST /v2/workspaces              # create (recipe, refresh, pool)
GET  /v2/workspaces/:id          # recipe, pool status, latest build
GET  /v2/workspaces/:id/builds   # lineage
POST /v2/workspaces/:id/builds   # build now
```

---

# Tigris cutover runbook

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/blobstore-tigris-cutover.md

# Tigris cutover runbook

Zero-downtime migration of all worker object storage (checkpoints,
hibernation archives, templates, goldens) from Azure Blob to Tigris using
`internal/blobstore.FallbackStore` in migration mode as the safety net during
the soak window.

> **Why not Tigris shadow buckets?** Tigris shadow buckets require an
> S3-compatible source endpoint. Azure Blob has no native S3 API, so shadow
> buckets don't apply without a separate S3↔Azure gateway. `FallbackStore`
> accomplishes the same goal (transparent fallback on cold reads) entirely
> in-process — no extra infrastructure.

## What this covers

| Data | Old backend | Cutover mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Checkpoints / hibernation archives / templates | Azure Blob | rclone bulk copy + FallbackStore in migration mode |
| Goldens — existing (`bases/<old-versions>/default.ext4`) | Azure Blob | rclone bulk copy (they live in the same container as checkpoints) |
| Goldens — new ones produced by future AMI bakes | Azure Blob | **AMI bake dual-writes to both Azure and Tigris** until Phase 5 |
| pg-backups / pg-wal | Azure Blob | Out of scope (managed by separate path) |

All worker-managed paths flow through `internal/blobstore.Store`, so a
single set of env-var changes switches them all.

## How worker.env is sourced

Worker `/etc/opensandbox/worker.env` is **not** baked into the AMI. The
control plane generates it per-VM at spawn time from its own `cfg`
(loaded from `/etc/opensandbox/server.env` on the CP):

```
server.env on CP  →  CP cfg  →  workerEnv template  →  cloud-init userdata  →  worker.env on each VM
```

Practical consequence: **for env-var-only changes, you edit `server.env`
on the CP and cycle workers. No AMI rebake needed.** AMI rebakes are only
required for binary or system-level changes.

> The `workerEnv` template lives in `cmd/server/main.go`. If you add new
> env vars that workers need, the template must be updated to propagate
> them. This PR added `OPENSANDBOX_S3_FALLBACK_*` and
> `OPENSANDBOX_BLOB_MIGRATION_MODE` to the template.

## Pre-flight inventory (prod, opencomputer-prod RG, eastus2)

- Storage account: `occkpt3ccf3c31`
- `checkpoints` container: ~1,854 blobs, ~2.08 TB (includes goldens in
  `bases/<hash>/default.ext4`)
- `pg-backups` / `pg-wal`: managed by postgres infra, not part of this cutover

## Tigris target

- Bucket: `opencomputer-prod` (Region Earth or `iad`, snapshots enabled)
- Layout: identical to Azure — rclone copies keys verbatim; no key
  rewriting required
- Per-backend bucket override is available: primary uses Tigris bucket
  `opencomputer-prod`, fallback uses Azure container `checkpoints`,
  configured via `OPENSANDBOX_S3_FALLBACK_BUCKET`

## Phase 1 — Ship the new binary + start dual-writing goldens

**Goal**: get the new code into the worker pool AND start uploading each
new AMI's golden to Tigris in parallel with Azure. No worker behavior
change yet (`OPENSANDBOX_S3_FALLBACK_*` unset means workers log "no
fallback" and behave identically to before).

1. Before merging: stash Tigris creds in GitHub Actions secrets used by
   `build-worker-ami.yml`:
   - `TIGRIS_ENDPOINT` = `https://t3.storage.dev`
   - `TIGRIS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` = `tid_...`
   - `TIGRIS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` = `tsec_...`
   - `TIGRIS_GOLDENS_BUCKET` = `opencomputer-prod`
2. Merge the PR.
3. CI builds a new worker AMI. The bake now performs **two** golden
   uploads:
   - Existing Python step → Azure container `checkpoints` (unchanged)
   - New step → Tigris bucket `opencomputer-prod` via
     `opensandbox-worker golden-upload` (skips silently if Tigris secrets
     aren't set, so this is safe on dev/PR branches that don't have them)
4. CI bumps KV `worker-image-version`. Scaler does rolling-replace.
5. Verify all workers report the new version via `GET /api/workers`.
6. Smoke test: create / hibernate / wake. Behavior identical.
7. Verify the new golden landed in Tigris:
   ```
   tigris ls "opencomputer-prod/bases/$(<the hash from packer output>)/"
   ```
   Should show `default.ext4` at the expected size.

**Rollback**: bump KV `worker-image-version` back. Scaler rolls back. The
Tigris-uploaded golden stays in Tigris as a no-op (no reader yet).

## Phase 2 — Bulk rclone Azure → Tigris

**Goal**: get ~all checkpoint data into Tigris before flipping. Workers
still on Azure — zero production impact.

1. Run `scripts/rclone-azure-to-tigris.sh` from a bastion VM in eastus2.
   - ~2 TB, ~1-3 hours on D4-class network (depends on bastion size)
2. Required rclone flags (already in the script):
   - `--s3-storage-class STANDARD` — Tigris rejects Azure's `Hot`/`Cool`
     tier names; force STANDARD or every PUT fails with 400 InvalidStorageClass
   - `--metadata=false` — skip Azure-specific metadata to avoid edge-case
     translation issues
3. Parity check when done:
   ```
   rclone size az:checkpoints
   rclone size tigris:opencomputer-prod
   ```
   Sizes should match within a small delta (new writes during the run).

**Rollback**: nothing to undo. Abandon Tigris copy; costs nothing.

## Phase 3 — Atomic flip (server.env + CP restart + worker cycle)

**Goal**: workers start writing to Tigris and reading Tigris-then-Azure.

1. **Delta rclone sync** — run again right before the next step. Picks
   up anything written to Azure since Phase 2. Should be fast (minutes).

2. **Edit `/etc/opensandbox/server.env`** on the control plane to add the
   Tigris primary, Azure fallback, and migration-mode flag:
   ```
   # Primary: Tigris
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_ENDPOINT=https://t3.storage.dev
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_BUCKET=opencomputer-prod
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_REGION=auto
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE=true
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<tigris key>
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<tigris secret>

   # Fallback: Azure
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_FALLBACK_ENDPOINT=https://occkpt3ccf3c31.blob.core.windows.net
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_FALLBACK_REGION=eastus2
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_FALLBACK_ACCESS_KEY_ID=occkpt3ccf3c31
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_FALLBACK_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<azure key>
   OPENSANDBOX_S3_FALLBACK_BUCKET=checkpoints

   # Lazy-migration: Tigris-miss falls through to Azure
   OPENSANDBOX_BLOB_MIGRATION_MODE=true
   ```

3. **Restart the control plane**:
   ```
   systemctl restart opensandbox-server
   ```
   Re-reads `server.env`. From now on, every new worker spawned by the
   scaler is templated with the new env via cloud-init.

4. **Cycle workers** — two options:
   - **Soft (gradual)**: do nothing. Existing workers keep their old env
     until the scaler cycles them (could be hours/days). Mixed pool during
     the window is fine — cross-worker ops still work because the
     new-config workers can fallback-read whatever the old-config workers
     wrote. The reverse direction (new writes Tigris, old needs to read)
     is avoided by the scaler's drain semantics — old workers are drained,
     not given new placements.
   - **Aggressive (forced)**: delete workers one at a time via
     `az vm delete -g opencomputer-prod -n osb-worker-<id>`. Scaler
     replaces each with a new VM that gets the new env. Whole pool
     flipped in minutes.

5. **Verify** as each worker cycles, log line:
   ```
   checkpoint store: tigris primary, azure-blob-fallback fallback (migration=true)
   ```

**Rollback**: revert `server.env`, restart CP, cycle workers. Data
already in Tigris stays there (passive replica); Azure remains
authoritative throughout the soak window.

## Phase 4 — Soak (1–2 weeks)

Monitor:
- Worker logs for `blobstore: primary tigris failed (...); trying fallback azure-blob` — expected near-zero and trending down as the warm working set lands in Tigris.
- Tigris dashboard: error rate, latency, ingress volume.
- Synthetic daily test: create / checkpoint / fork on another worker / hibernate / wake.

If fallback hit rate stays elevated, run another delta rclone sync to
warm cold keys into Tigris proactively.

## Phase 5 — Disable fallback + drop Azure golden upload (commit to Tigris)

1. Edit `server.env`: remove the `OPENSANDBOX_S3_FALLBACK_*` block and
   `OPENSANDBOX_BLOB_MIGRATION_MODE`.
2. Restart CP.
3. Cycle workers (same options as Phase 3 step 4).
4. Verify log: `checkpoint store: tigris primary (no fallback)`.
5. **Remove the Python Azure-upload step from `deploy/packer/worker-ami.pkr.hcl`.**
   At this point Tigris is the authoritative store and Azure shouldn't
   receive new writes. The Tigris-upload step stays.
6. Optionally also remove the "download previous golden from Azure" step
   and replace with a Tigris fetch (or accept the runtime fetch cost for
   forks of stale-pinned checkpoints, which should be rare).

**Rollback past this point** is harder. Re-adding the fallback re-enables
the safety net, but any keys written to Tigris during the no-fallback
window don't exist in Azure. If Azure must become authoritative again,
run a reverse rclone (Tigris → Azure). Don't enter this phase until
Phase 4 has been clean for at least a week.

## Phase 6 — Decommission Azure

After ~30 days of zero observed reads on the Azure side (verify via Azure
storage metrics):

1. Snapshot the `checkpoints` container to a different storage account
   as a one-time backup (optional).
2. `az storage container delete --account-name occkpt3ccf3c31 -n checkpoints`
3. Eventually delete the storage account.

## Operational rules

- **Never `systemctl restart opensandbox-worker` by hand in prod.** The
  scaler treats the heartbeat gap as "worker unhealthy" and replaces the
  VM from the current AMI — losing any local state. We hit this during
  dev validation. Always cycle workers by deleting them so the scaler
  replaces them cleanly.

- **Don't hold the leader lock in prod.** Holding
  `controlplane:leader = MAINTENANCE-HOLD` pauses the scaler — including
  the rolling-replace that the cutover relies on. The lock trick is for
  one-off dev hot-swaps only.

- **Live migration during the rolling window works** because the new
  workers are in migration mode. Drain direction is OLD → NEW: old
  worker writes drives to Azure, new worker reads Tigris (miss) →
  fallback to Azure (hit) → migration succeeds. The reverse direction
  (NEW writes, OLD reads) doesn't happen — old workers are being
  drained, not receiving new placements.

## Code surface

- `internal/blobstore/store.go` — `Store` interface (Get / GetRange / Put / Head / Exists / Delete / Name)
- `internal/blobstore/s3.go` — S3-compatible backend (Tigris, R2, AWS S3, MinIO); supports per-backend `Bucket` override
- `internal/blobstore/azure.go` — Azure Blob backend; same `Bucket` override pattern
- `internal/blobstore/fallback.go` — `FallbackStore` with `NewFallback` (HA mode) and `NewMigrationFallback` (lazy-migration mode)
- `internal/storage/s3.go` — `CheckpointStore` higher-level type, built on top of `blobstore.Store`
- `cmd/server/main.go` — `workerEnv` template propagates `OPENSANDBOX_S3_FALLBACK_*` and `OPENSANDBOX_BLOB_MIGRATION_MODE` to each spawned worker
- `cmd/worker/main.go` — `buildCheckpointBackend` helper; combines primary + fallback for the checkpoint path
- `internal/config/config.go` — env-var parsing for the new vars
- `scripts/rclone-azure-to-tigris.sh` — bulk + delta rclone driver (with `--s3-storage-class STANDARD --metadata=false`)

---

# Log in or update session state, then delete the browser.

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/browser-sessions/overview.mdx

title: "Browser Sessions"
description: "Preview: create cloud browser sessions for Playwright, Magnitude, and profile-backed web automation"

<Warning>
Browser Sessions are currently in invite-only preview. Access is enabled for
approved organizations, and API routes, SDK method names, response fields,
limits, and pricing may change before general availability.
</Warning>

Browser Sessions create managed Chromium sessions for web agents and browser
automation. OpenComputer handles API-key auth and org ownership, then returns
browser connection URLs for tools such as Playwright and Magnitude.

If your organization has not been invited to the preview, Browser Session API
calls may fail even when your OpenComputer API key is valid.

Use Browser Sessions when you want a cloud browser without installing Chromium
inside an OpenComputer sandbox. Use [sandboxes](/sandboxes/overview) when you
need a full Linux VM with your own browser runtime and filesystem.

## Create a Browser

<CodeGroup>

```typescript TypeScript
import { Browser } from "@opencomputer/sdk";

const browser = await Browser.create({
  headless: false,
  stealth: true,
  startUrl: "https://example.com",
  timeoutSeconds: 120,
});

console.log(browser.id);
console.log(browser.cdpWsUrl);
console.log(browser.liveViewUrl);

await browser.delete();
```

```python Python
from opencomputer import Browser

browser = await Browser.create(
    headless=False,
    stealth=True,
    start_url="https://example.com",
    timeout_seconds=120,
)

print(browser.id)
print(browser.cdp_ws_url)
print(browser.live_view_url)

await browser.delete()
```

</CodeGroup>

Headful browsers return a live-view URL. Headless browsers are lighter, but do
not provide a live view.

## Playwright

The browser response includes a CDP WebSocket URL. Pass it directly to
Playwright's `connectOverCDP`.

<CodeGroup>

```typescript TypeScript
import { Browser } from "@opencomputer/sdk";
import { chromium } from "playwright";

const ocBrowser = await Browser.create({
  headless: false,
  startUrl: "https://example.com",
});

try {
  const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP(ocBrowser.cdpWsUrl);
  const context = browser.contexts()[0] || await browser.newContext();
  const page = context.pages()[0] || await context.newPage();

  await page.goto("https://example.com");
  console.log(await page.title());

  await browser.close();
} finally {
  await ocBrowser.delete();
}
```

```python Python
from opencomputer import Browser
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright

oc_browser = await Browser.create(
    headless=False,
    start_url="https://example.com",
)

try:
    async with async_playwright() as p:
        browser = await p.chromium.connect_over_cdp(oc_browser.cdp_ws_url)
        context = browser.contexts[0] if browser.contexts else await browser.new_context()
        page = context.pages[0] if context.pages else await context.new_page()

        await page.goto("https://example.com")
        print(await page.title())

        await browser.close()
finally:
    await oc_browser.delete()
```

</CodeGroup>

## Magnitude

Magnitude can use a Playwright-connected browser. Create the OpenComputer
browser first, connect over CDP, then hand the page to your Magnitude agent.

```typescript TypeScript
import { Browser } from "@opencomputer/sdk";
import { chromium } from "playwright";
import { startBrowserAgent } from "magnitude-core";

const ocBrowser = await Browser.create({
  headless: false,
  stealth: true,
  startUrl: "https://example.com",
});

try {
  const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP(ocBrowser.cdpWsUrl);
  const context = browser.contexts()[0] || await browser.newContext();
  const page = context.pages()[0] || await context.newPage();

  const agent = await startBrowserAgent({ page });
  await agent.act("Find the page title and summarize what this site is for.");

  await browser.close();
} finally {
  await ocBrowser.delete();
}
```

<Note>
Magnitude package names and constructors can vary by version. The
OpenComputer-specific step is stable: create a `Browser`, connect to
`cdpWsUrl` with Playwright, then pass the resulting page or browser object to
Magnitude.
</Note>

## Save and Load Profiles

Profiles persist browser state such as cookies and local storage across browser
sessions. Profiles are scoped to your OpenComputer org; another org cannot
list, load, or delete your profiles.

Create a profile once:

<CodeGroup>

```typescript TypeScript
import { BrowserProfile } from "@opencomputer/sdk";

const profile = await BrowserProfile.create({
  name: "github-login",
});
```

```python Python
from opencomputer import BrowserProfile

profile = await BrowserProfile.create(name="github-login")
```

</CodeGroup>

Use the profile when creating a browser:

<CodeGroup>

```typescript TypeScript
import { Browser } from "@opencomputer/sdk";

const browser = await Browser.create({
  profile: {
    id: profile.id,
    saveChanges: true,
  },
  headless: false,
});

// Log in or update session state, then delete the browser.
// With saveChanges enabled, changes are saved back to the profile.
await browser.delete();
```

```python Python
from opencomputer import Browser

browser = await Browser.create(
    profile={
        "id": profile.id,
        "save_changes": True,
    },
    headless=False,
)

# Log in or update session state, then delete the browser.
# With save_changes enabled, changes are saved back to the profile.
await browser.delete()
```

</CodeGroup>

Load the same profile later by ID or name:

<CodeGroup>

```typescript TypeScript
import { Browser, BrowserProfile } from "@opencomputer/sdk";

const profile = await BrowserProfile.connect("github-login");

const browser = await Browser.create({
  profile: {
    id: profile.id,
    saveChanges: true,
  },
  headless: false,
});
```

```python Python
from opencomputer import Browser, BrowserProfile

profile = await BrowserProfile.connect("github-login")

browser = await Browser.create(
    profile={
        "id": profile.id,
        "save_changes": True,
    },
    headless=False,
)
```

</CodeGroup>

## Authentication

The SDK uses your OpenComputer API key:

```bash
export OPENCOMPUTER_API_KEY="osb_..."
```

<Note>
For local development against a non-production Browser Sessions endpoint, set
`OPENCOMPUTER_BROWSER_API_URL`.
</Note>

---

# or using the shortcut:

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/cli/checkpoint.mdx

title: "Checkpoints"
description: "Snapshot, fork, and restore from the CLI"

## Creating a Checkpoint

Capture the current state of a running sandbox:

```bash
oc checkpoint create sb-abc123 --name before-migration
# or using the shortcut:
oc cp create sb-abc123 --name before-migration
```

The checkpoint saves the filesystem and installed state. Status starts as `processing` and transitions to `ready`.

```bash
oc cp list sb-abc123
# ID          NAME               STATUS  SIZE     CREATED
# cp-7f3a1b2c before-migration   ready   128 MB   2025-01-15T10:30:00Z
```

## Forking from a Checkpoint

Create new sandboxes from a saved checkpoint. Each fork is independent:

```bash
# Spawn two independent sandboxes from the same checkpoint
ID1=$(oc cp spawn cp-7f3a1b2c --json | jq -r '.sandboxID')
ID2=$(oc cp spawn cp-7f3a1b2c --json | jq -r '.sandboxID')

# Run different experiments
oc exec $ID1 --wait -- ./experiment-a.sh
oc exec $ID2 --wait -- ./experiment-b.sh
```

Forked sandboxes start with a fresh boot from the saved disk state — don't assume running processes carry over.

## Restoring

Revert a sandbox in-place to a checkpoint. All changes since the checkpoint are lost:

```bash
oc cp restore sb-abc123 cp-7f3a1b2c
```

## Listing and Deleting

```bash
oc cp list sb-abc123
oc cp delete sb-abc123 cp-7f3a1b2c
```

Each sandbox can have up to 10 full checkpoints and up to 100 disk-only checkpoints.

To create a new checkpoint at the limit, opt into automatic deletion of the oldest eligible checkpoint of the same type:

```bash
oc cp create sb-abc123 \
  --name autosave \
  --kind disk_only \
  --retention-policy delete_oldest \
  --retention-max-count 100
```

Retention skips public checkpoints, patched checkpoints, and checkpoints that are still referenced by forked sandboxes.

## Checkpoint vs Hibernate

| | Checkpoint | Hibernate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original sandbox | Keeps running | Stopped |
| Can fork | Yes — unlimited new sandboxes | No |
| Use case | Branching, parallel testing | Pause and resume, cost savings |

Use checkpoints when you need to explore multiple paths from the same state. Use hibernation when you just want to pause and resume later.

<Tip>
  SDK usage: [Checkpoints](/sandboxes/checkpoints). Full flags: [CLI Reference](/reference/cli#oc-checkpoint).
</Tip>

---

# → Session es-xyz created. Attach with: oc exec attach sb-abc es-xyz

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/cli/exec.mdx

title: "Running Commands"
description: "Execute shell commands from the CLI"

## Running a Command

Use `--wait` to run a command synchronously — output streams to your terminal and the CLI exits with the process exit code:

```bash
oc exec sb-abc123 --wait -- echo "Hello, World!"
oc exec sb-abc123 --wait -- npm run build
```

Without `--wait`, `oc exec` creates an **exec session** and prints the session ID with attach instructions. This is useful for long-running commands:

```bash
oc exec sb-abc123 -- node server.js
# → Session es-xyz created. Attach with: oc exec attach sb-abc es-xyz
```

## Working Directory & Environment

```bash
oc exec sb-abc123 --wait --cwd /app --env NODE_ENV=production -- npm run build
oc exec sb-abc123 --wait --env API_KEY=xxx --env DEBUG=true -- ./run.sh
```

## Timeouts

Set a timeout with `--timeout` (in seconds). Default is 0 (no timeout). When exceeded, the command is killed:

```bash
oc exec sb-abc123 --wait --timeout 30 -- npm test
```

## Creating an Exec Session

Plain `oc exec` (without `--wait`) creates a session for long-running commands. The command keeps running even after you disconnect:

```bash
oc exec sb-abc123 -- python train.py
# Session es-abc created
```

## Capturing Output as JSON

Combine `--json` with `--wait` for scripting:

```bash
RESULT=$(oc exec sb-abc123 --json --wait -- node -e 'console.log("hello")')
echo $RESULT | jq '.stdout'   # "hello\n"
echo $RESULT | jq '.exitCode' # 0
```

## Managing Exec Sessions

```bash
# List active sessions
oc exec list sb-abc123

# Kill a session
oc exec kill sb-abc123 es-xyz
oc exec kill sb-abc123 es-xyz --signal 15  # SIGTERM
```

<Warning>
  `oc exec attach` exists as a command but is not yet implemented. It prints guidance to use the SDK or a WebSocket client. Use `oc exec list` and `oc exec kill` to manage sessions from the CLI.
</Warning>

## Shell vs Exec

| Use Case | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Single command, capture output | `oc exec --wait` |
| Scripting and automation | `oc exec --wait --json` |
| Long-running background process | `oc exec` (no `--wait`) |
| Interactive development, debugging | [`oc shell`](/cli/shell) |

<Tip>
  SDK usage: [Running Commands](/sandboxes/running-commands). Full flags: [CLI Reference](/reference/cli#oc-exec).
</Tip>

---

# Create a sandbox

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/cli/overview.mdx

title: "CLI"
description: "Manage sandboxes from your terminal"

The `oc` CLI lets you manage OpenComputer sandboxes directly from your terminal — create sandboxes, run commands, open interactive shells, manage checkpoints, and more.

## Installation

<CodeGroup>

```bash macOS (Apple Silicon)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/releases/latest/download/oc-darwin-arm64 -o /usr/local/bin/oc
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/oc
```

```bash macOS (Intel)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/releases/latest/download/oc-darwin-amd64 -o /usr/local/bin/oc
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/oc
```

```bash Linux (x86_64)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/releases/latest/download/oc-linux-amd64 -o /usr/local/bin/oc
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/oc
```

```bash Linux (ARM64)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/releases/latest/download/oc-linux-arm64 -o /usr/local/bin/oc
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/oc
```

</CodeGroup>

## Configuration

```bash
oc config set api-key your-api-key
oc config show
```

### Resolution Order

| Priority | Source | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (highest) | CLI flags | `--api-key=xxx` |
| 2 | Environment variables | `OPENCOMPUTER_API_KEY` |
| 3 | Config file | `~/.oc/config.json` |
| 4 (lowest) | Defaults | `https://app.opencomputer.dev` |

## Global Flags

| Flag | Environment Variable | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--api-key` | `OPENCOMPUTER_API_KEY` | API key for authentication |
| `--api-url` | `OPENCOMPUTER_API_URL` | Control plane URL |
| `--json` | — | Output as JSON instead of tables |

## Key Workflows

### Quick Start

```bash
# Create a sandbox
oc create

# Run a command and wait for the result
oc exec sb-abc123 --wait -- echo "Hello from the cloud"

# Open an interactive shell
oc shell sb-abc123

# Clean up
oc sandbox kill sb-abc123
```

### JSON Output & Scripting

All commands support `--json` for machine-readable output:

```bash
# Get a sandbox ID programmatically
ID=$(oc create --json | jq -r '.sandboxID')

# List all running sandbox IDs
oc ls --json | jq -r '.[].sandboxID'

# Run a command and capture the result
RESULT=$(oc exec $ID --json --wait -- npm test)
echo $RESULT | jq '.exitCode'
```

### Top-level Shortcuts

| Shortcut | Expands to |
| --- | --- |
| `oc create` | `oc sandbox create` |
| `oc ls` | `oc sandbox list` |
| `oc cp` | `oc checkpoint` |

### Create and Shell In

```bash
oc shell $(oc create --json | jq -r '.sandboxID')
```

### Hibernate for Cost Savings

```bash
oc sandbox hibernate sb-abc123
# ... hours later ...
oc sandbox wake sb-abc123
oc shell sb-abc123
```

### Checkpoint and Fork

```bash
oc cp create sb-abc --name ready-state
ID1=$(oc cp spawn cp-xyz --json | jq -r '.sandboxID')
ID2=$(oc cp spawn cp-xyz --json | jq -r '.sandboxID')
oc exec $ID1 --wait -- ./test-a.sh
oc exec $ID2 --wait -- ./test-b.sh
```

## Command Reference

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [`oc sandbox`](/cli/sandbox) | Create, list, kill, hibernate, wake |
| [`oc exec`](/cli/exec) | Run commands, manage exec sessions |
| [`oc shell`](/cli/shell) | Interactive PTY terminal |
| [`oc checkpoint`](/cli/checkpoint) | Snapshot, fork, restore |
| [`oc patch`](/cli/patch) | Checkpoint-attached scripts |
| [`oc preview`](/cli/preview) | Expose ports to the internet |
| [`oc config`](/reference/cli#oc-config) | Configure API key and API URL |

<Tip>
  Full flag reference for every command: [CLI Reference](/reference/cli).
</Tip>

# From a file

Source: https://github.com/diggerhq/opencomputer/blob/main/docs/cli/patch.mdx

title: "Patches"
description: "Attach scripts to checkpoints from the CLI"

## What Patches Do

A patch is a shell script attached to a checkpoint. Patches run in order every time a sandbox is forked from that checkpoint — layer setup without re-creating the checkpoint.

## Creating a Patch

From a file or stdin:

```bash
# From a file
oc patch create cp-7f3a1b2c --script ./setup.sh --description "Install deps"

# One-liner from stdin
echo "npm install -g typescript" | oc patch create cp-7f3a1b2c --script=-
```

## Layering Setup

Add multiple patches — they execute in creation order on every fork:

```bash
oc patch create cp-7f3a1b2c --script ./install-node.sh --description "Node.js 20"
oc patch create cp-7f3a1b2c --script ./app-config.sh --description "App config"

# Each spawned sandbox gets both patches applied in order
oc cp spawn cp-7f3a1b2c
```

## Inspecting Patches

Review what will run before forking:

```bash
oc patch list cp-7f3a1b2c
# ID          SEQ  DESCRIPTION     STRATEGY  CREATED
# pa-abc123   1    Node.js 20      on_wake   2025-01-15T10:30:00Z
# pa-def456   2    App config      on_wake   2025-01-15T10:31:00Z
```

## Removing a Patch

```bash
oc patch delete cp-7f3a1b2c pa-abc123
```

<Tip>
  SDK usage: [Patches](/sandboxes/patches). Full flags: [CLI Reference](/reference/cli#oc-patch).
</Tip>
